title: Biceps-related Shoulder Pain and Biceps Tendon Rupture
case: Case: A 58-year-old carpenter has 6 weeks of front shoulder pain with lifting and overhead work. The bicipital groove is tender. Speed's test reproduces his pain. Painful arc is mild, passive range is full, no apprehension, no neurological signs.

Working diagnosis: long head of biceps tendinopathy with possible mild cuff involvement. Plan: education, isometrics, slow loaded elbow flexion and cuff and scapular strengthening, graded return to overhead work.
qa: Why is Speed's test not definitive? It is also positive with other conditions and its accuracy is limited, so it must be combined with palpation and the rest of the examination.

A 62-year-old has a sudden pop and a Popeye bulge but keeps good strength. What is the usual approach? Proximal rupture is often managed without surgery in older, less demanding patients; reassure and rehabilitate [Ref - to verify].
Why check the elbow after a pop in the arm? A distal rupture changes urgency because earlier surgical review may be needed.
Why avoid steroid injection near the tendon? Some reports link it with tendon weakening and rupture [Ref - to verify].
Why is heart pain on the list? Front shoulder or arm pain can come from the heart and must be excluded in the right history.

fields.Purpose: Check for pain in the bicipital groove when the biceps is loaded with the shoulder flexed
fields.Position: Standing or sitting; arm forward at about 90 degrees, elbow extended, forearm supinated (palm up)
fields.Action: The therapist applies a downward force at the forearm while the patient resists
fields.Positive: Pain in the bicipital groove or front of the shoulder (familiar pain)
fields.Supports: LHB involvement, together with groove tenderness
fields.Limits: Also positive with cuff and labral problems [Ref - to verify]

fields.Purpose: Load the biceps in supination with the tendon in the groove
fields.Position: Sitting; elbow bent to 90 degrees at the side, forearm pronated
fields.Action: The patient actively supinates and externally rotates against the therapist's resistance
fields.Positive: Pain in the bicipital groove, sometimes a click
fields.Limits: Low accuracy; not specific [Ref - to verify]

redFlags.Finding: Sudden pop at the elbow with weak forearm supination and flexion, young or active person
redFlags.Why it matters: Distal tendon rupture; surgery timing matters

redFlags.Finding: Proximal rupture with severe weakness or in a high-demand worker or athlete
Numbness or weakness in the arm

manual.name: Soft-tissue work for surrounding muscles (pectoralis, deltoid, upper trapezius)
Direct deep friction over the tendon

manualNotes: Preferred starting choice: education and load-based exercise. Manual therapy is a minor adjunct only. Do not claim that manual therapy repairs the tendon.

exercise.Exercise: Isometric elbow flexion with the arm at the side
exercise.Steps: Sitting, elbow bent to 90 degrees, push the wrist up into the other hand or a surface
exercise.Starting dose: 5 holds of 30 to 45 seconds [Ref - to verify]
exercise.Regress when: Pain stays high into the next day

exercise.Steps: Light dumbbell, 3 seconds up, 3 seconds down

exerciseNotes: Symptom rule: pain up to about 3 to 4 out of 10 that settles within a day is acceptable. Avoid heavy pulling or lifting at end range until pain settles.

After proximal rupture: most people recover good function with rehabilitation. Start with pain-guided movement, then strengthening of the remaining muscles and a graded return to lifting. Tell the patient that the bulge usually remains [Ref - to verify].
Distal rupture or surgery: follow the surgeon's protocol.

modalities.name: Corticosteroid injection near the tendon
modalities.comment: Use with caution; tendon rupture risk discussed in some reports [Ref - to verify]

pathway: Emergency or urgent flag? Yes: act as in Section G.
Sudden pop with bulge in the upper arm? Yes: suspect rupture. Check the elbow for distal rupture, and refer as needed.
Front shoulder pain with groove tenderness, positive Speed or Yergason, no instability or cuff weakness? Yes: working diagnosis is LHB tendinopathy, often with associated cuff problems.
Other findings suggest labral or subscapularis problems? Yes: refer for further assessment.
Visit 1: screen flags, check for rupture, explain the likely cause and plan.
Early: reduce painful pulling and lifting, begin isometrics.
Middle: slow loaded strengthening, cuff and scapular work.
